fetched_contents.text: Clinical endoscopic management and outcome of post-endoscopic sphincterotomy bleeding Abstract Post-endoscopic sphincterotomy bleeding is a common complication of biliary sphincterotomy, and the incidence varies from 1% to 48%. It can be challenging to localize the bleeder or to administer various interventions through a side-viewing endoscope. This study aimed to evaluate the risk factors of post-endoscopic sphincterotomy bleeding and the outcome of endoscopic intervention therapies. We retrospectively reviewed the records of 513 patients who underwent biliary sphincterotomy in Mackay Memorial Hospital between 2011 and 2016. The blood biochemistry, comorbidities, indication for sphincterotomy, severity of bleeding, endoscopic features of bleeder, and type of endoscopic therapy were analyzed. Post-endoscopic sphincterotomy bleeding occurred in 65 (12.6%) patients. Forty-five patients had immediate bleeding and 20 patients had delayed bleeding. The multivariate analysis of risk factors associated with post-endoscopic sphincterotomy bleeding were liver cirrhosis (P = 0.029), end-stage renal disease (P = 0.038), previous antiplatelet drug use (P<0.001), and duodenal ulcer (P = 0.023). The complications of pancreatitis and cholangitis were higher in the bleeding group, with statistical significance. Delayed bleeding occurred within 1 to 7 days (mean, 2.5 days), and 60% (12/20) of the patients received endoscopic evaluation. In the delayed bleeding group, the successful hemostasis rate was 71.4% (5/7), and 65% (13/20) of the patients had ceased bleeding without endoscopic hemostasis therapy. Comparison of different therapeutic modalities showed that cholangitis was higher in patients who received epinephrine spray (P = 0.042) and pancreatitis was higher in patients who received epinephrine injection and electrocoagulation (P = 0.041 and P = 0.039 respectively). Clinically, post-endoscopic sphincterotomy bleeding and further endoscopic hemostasis therapy increase the complication rate of pancreatitis and cholangitis. Realizing the effectiveness of each therapeutic modalities and appropriate management of different levels bleeding are important. Introduction Endoscopic sphincterotomy (ES) is the cornerstone of therapeutic endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) for accessing the biliary and pancreatic ductal systems. Bleeding is one of the most frequent complications following ES [1]. The incidence varies from 1% to 48% depending on what definition is applied, specifically whether bleeding during the procedure is included [1–4]. It varies between self-limiting and life-threatening bleeding and is occasionally associated with a considerable mortality rate of 0.3% [3]. The timing of delayed post-ES bleeding may be immediate or up to 10 days following ES [2, 5]. A small amount of post-ES bleeding is common and most often resolves spontaneously [1]. Thus, endoscopic therapy was suggested to be undertaken for the treatment of “endoscopically significant” immediate bleeding or “clinically significant” delayed bleeding [1]. However, some cases present with significant bleeding that requires blood transfusions and urgent endoscopic intervention, such as injection, balloon tamponade, thermal, and mechanical methods—alone or in combination [6–9]. If refractory bleeding occurs, repeated endoscopic hemostatic therapy, angiographic embolization, or surgery is required [3, 4]. Owing to the tangential approach in these patients, the bleeding could not be handled easily with side-viewing endoscope and this urgent procedure could not be practically performed by the gastroenterologists experienced in ERCP each time. Furthermore, bleeding that obscures the visual field makes identification of the precise location in delayed bleeding impossible. The complications of pancreatitis, cholangitis, and cholecystitis associated with endoscopic hemostasis were higher in patients who underwent endoscopic hemostasis than in patients who did not undergo endoscopic hemostasis [10]. There are a few series that specifically describe effectiveness and complication of endoscopic hemostasis for post-ES bleeding [1, 7, 10, 11]. Therefore, the primary endpoint of this study was to evaluate the risk factors of post-ES bleeding. The secondary endpoint was to evaluate the efficacy and outcome of different endoscopic intervention therapies for post-ES bleeding. Materials and methods Patients selection and data collection Five hundred thirteen patients who underwent ES at Mackay Memorial Hospital, Taipei Medical Center, between January 2011 and August 2016, were enrolled. All ES procedures were performed by four experienced endoscopists (experienced endoscopist as a specialist in ERCP with a minimum of 3 years post-training experience), and the decision to perform sphincterotomy was based on clinical, endoscopic, and radiologic findings. None of the participants used anticoagulants or antiplatelet agents from 3 days before or until 3 days after ERCP. Prophylactic antibiotic or rectal indomethacin was not prescribed in any of the patient. This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Mackay Memorial Hospital (reference number: 17MMHIS024) and waived the requirement for informed consent because the current study was retrospective in design. Patient information was anonymized and de-identified prior to analysis. INTRODUCTION Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is an advanced endoscopic procedure in which a specialized side-viewing upper endoscope is guided into the duodenum, allowing for instruments to be passed through the ampulla of Vater and into the biliary and pancreatic ducts. The role of ERCP in managing pancreaticobiliary disorders is mostly a therapeutic one because other accurate methods of diagnostic testing (eg, magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography, endoscopic ultrasound [EUS]) are available without the risks associated with ERCP. Bleeding is a serious adverse event related to ERCP, and it is most often observed after biliary or pancreatic sphincterotomy. Less common causes of bleeding include splenic, hepatic or vascular injury, endoscopic stenting or tissue sampling, and submucosal bleeding of the papilla in patients at higher risk for bleeding (eg, those with a hemostatic disorder). Because of advances in equipment, preventive techniques, and endoscopic training, ERCP-related bleeding has become relatively less common over time. This topic will discuss preventive strategies and treatment of bleeding related to ERCP. fetched_contents.text: Selective Embolization for Post-Endoscopic Sphincterotomy Bleeding: Technical Aspects and Clinical Efficacy Abstract Objective The objective of this study was to evaluate the technical aspects and clinical efficacy of selective embolization for post-endoscopic sphincterotomy bleeding. Materials and Methods We reviewed the records of 10 patients (3%; M:F = 6:4; mean age, 63.3 years) that underwent selective embolization for post-endoscopic sphincterotomy bleeding among 344 patients who received arteriography for nonvariceal upper gastrointestinal bleeding from 2000 to 2009. We analyzed the endoscopic procedure, onset of bleeding, underlying clinical condition, angiographic findings, interventional procedure, and outcomes in these patients. Results Among the 12 bleeding branches, primary success of hemostasis was achieved in 10 bleeding branches (83%). Secondary success occurred in two additional bleeding branches (100%) after repeated embolization. In 10 patients, post-endoscopic sphincterotomy bleedings were detected during the endoscopic procedure (n = 2, 20%) or later (n = 8, 80%), and the delay was from one to eight days (mean, 2.9 days; ± 2.3). Coagulopathy was observed in three patients. Eight patients had a single bleeding branch, whereas two patients had two branches. On the selective arteriography, bleeding branches originated from the posterior pancreaticoduodenal artery (n = 8, 67%) and anterior pancreaticoduodenal artery (n = 4, 33%), respectively. Superselection was achieved in four branches and the embolization was performed with n-butyl cyanoacrylate. The eight branches were embolized by combined use of coil, n-butyl cyanoacrylate, or Gelfoam. After the last embolization, there was no rebleeding or complication related to embolization. Conclusion Selective embolization is technically feasible and an effective procedure for post-endoscopic sphincterotomy bleeding. In addition, the posterior pancreaticoduodenal artery is the main origin of the causative vessels of post-endoscopic sphincterotomy bleeding. Keywords: Bleeding, Embolization, Pancreaticoduodenal artery, Sphincterotomy INTRODUCTION Bleeding after endoscopic sphincterotomy (ES) is one of the most frequent complications of endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP), and has been reported in 1-10% of patients. Most post-ES bleedings stop spontaneously, but significant bleeding may occur during the procedure or several days later. Post-ES bleeding is rarely encountered by interventional radiologists, unlike other nonvariceal upper gastrointestinal bleeding, because various hemostatic procedures are performed simultaneously or repeatedly during the endoscopic procedure. However, in cases of endoscopic hemostasis failure caused by massive bleeding or technical failure, radiologic or surgical hemostasis may be required (1-3). According to previous reports, since the duodenum has a rich vascular network, rebleeding after embolization is common when the embolization has been performed incompletely or coagulopathy has existed (4, 5). On the other hand, embolization may cause ischemic complications of the duodenum when the gastroduodenal artery is embolized or the patient has had surgically altered anatomy (4, 6). Therefore, selective embolization of bleeding branch for post-ES bleeding is required to reduce rebleeding or ischemic complication related to embolization. However, only a few reports have addressed the endovascular management of post-ES bleeding and these reports have shown limited evaluation for its technical aspect or clinical efficacy due to small study populations or the lack of analysis on post-ES bleeding (3, 4, 7). Thus, in this study we aimed to retrospectively evaluate the technical aspects and clinical efficacy of selective embolization of post-ES bleeding. MATERIALS AND METHODS Our Institutional Review Board approved this retrospective study and informed consent from the subjects was waived. We analyzed patient demographics, underlying diseases and clinical conditions of the patients, ES procedure, onset of bleeding, angiographic findings, interventional procedure and outcomes. Patients Between January 2000 and January 2009, embolizations for nonvariceal upper gastrointestinal bleeding were performed in 344 patients at our institute. fetched_contents.text: Predictors of re-bleeding after endoscopic hemostasis for delayed post-endoscopic sphincterotomy bleeding Abstract AIM: To predict the re-bleeding after endoscopic hemostasis for delayed post-endoscopic sphincterotomy (ES) bleeding. METHODS: Over a 15-year period, data from 161 patients with delayed post-ES bleeding were retrospectively collected from a single medical center. To identify risk factors for re-bleeding after initial successful endoscopic hemostasis, parameters before, during and after the procedure of endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography were analyzed. These included age, gender, blood biochemistry, co-morbidities, endoscopic diagnosis, presence of peri-ampullary diverticulum, occurrence of immediate post-ES bleeding, use of needle knife precut sphincterotomy, severity of delayed bleeding, endoscopic features on delayed bleeding, and type of endoscopic therapy. RESULTS: A total of 35 patients (21.7%) had re-bleeding after initial successful endoscopic hemostasis for delayed post-ES bleeding. Univariate analysis revealed that malignant biliary stricture, serum bilirubin level of greater than 10 mg/dL, initial bleeding severity, and bleeding diathesis were significant predictors of re-bleeding. By multivariate analysis, serum bilirubin level of greater than 10 mg/dL and initial bleeding severity remained significant predictors. Re-bleeding was controlled by endoscopic therapy in a single (n = 23) or multiple (range, 2-7; n = 6) sessions in 29 of the 35 patients (82.9%). Four patients required transarterial embolization and one went for surgery. These five patients had severe bleeding when delayed post-ES bleeding occurred. One patient with decompensated liver cirrhosis died from re-bleeding. CONCLUSION: Re-bleeding occurs in approximately one-fifth of patients after initial successful endoscopic hemostasis for delayed post-ES bleeding. Severity of initial bleeding and serum bilirubin level of greater than 10 mg/dL are predictors of re-bleeding. Predictors of re-bleeding has not been studied. Our study reveals malignant biliary stricture, serum bilirubin level of greater than 10 mg/dL, initial bleeding severity, and bleeding diathesis were significant predictors of re-bleeding. These patients often require multiple endoscopic treatments, transarterial embolization or surgery to control the bleeding. Sphincterotomy wound bleeding is its most frequent complication[1,2]. The incidence of clinically significant post-ES bleeding ranges between 0.76%-2% when it is defined as overt gastrointestinal bleeding with decreased hemoglobin level[1,3-5]. The majority of immediate post-ES bleeding is self-limited and can usually be managed conservatively[9-11]. Wilcox et al[9] reported that the pattern of bleeding following ES does not predict the risk of delayed bleeding. Delayed post-ES bleeding occurs after the completion of ERCP[7]. These patients generally have clinical manifestations of overt gastrointestinal bleeding, such as melena, hematemesis, or hematochezia, and decreased hemoglobin level that require immediate endoscopic hemostasis[12-16]. Some patients re-bleed after initial successful treatment and need repeated endoscopic hemostatic therapy, transarterial embolization (TAE) or even surgery to control bleeding. However, factors affecting the success of endoscopic treatment for delayed post-ES bleeding has rarely been studied[17]. Determining the risk factors for re-bleeding after endoscopic treatment for delayed post-ES bleeding may be useful for monitoring or establishing additional hemostatic measures in high-risk patients. Branch report on hemostasis strategies and interventions

Endoscopic techniques remain the first-line approach for controlling post-endoscopic sphincterotomy (post-ES) bleeding. The evidence base highlights a range of endoscopic hemostatic methods, including epinephrine injection, thermal coagulation, mechanical clips, and over-the-scope clips. In the search results, UpToDate summarizes that “endoscopic evaluation” and “endoscopic methods for hemostasis” are central to management, and it notes that devices used for endoscopic hemostasis in the GI tract include injection devices, thermal devices, and clips or fully covered metallic stents [N2-R2][N6-R4]. Another source states that epinephrine injection, balloon tamponade, thermal coagulation, and endoscopic clips are foundational treatment modalities for post-sphincterotomy bleeding [N3-R2]. A dedicated review on endoscopic management also emphasizes that endoscopic therapy is suggested for “endoscopically significant” immediate bleeding or “clinically significant” delayed bleeding, and that injection, balloon tamponade, thermal, and mechanical methods—alone or in combination—are used for significant bleeding requiring blood transfusions and urgent endoscopic intervention [N1-F1].

The evidence also supports a stepwise or multimodal approach. The search result from the endoscopic management study says that “types of endoscopic therapy could be either monotherapy or combination therapy at the endoscopists' discretion” [N1-R3]. That same study reports that delayed bleeding occurred in 20 of 513 patients, with 60% receiving endoscopic evaluation, and that the successful hemostasis rate in the delayed bleeding group was 71.4% [N1-F1]. The same source also notes that complications such as pancreatitis and cholangitis were higher in patients who received epinephrine spray and in those who received epinephrine injection plus electrocoagulation [N1-F1]. This suggests that endoscopic choice should be balanced against the risk of adverse procedural complications.

For embolization, the evidence is more limited but still informative. The selective embolization study specifically addresses post-ES bleeding and reports that selective embolization is technically feasible and effective, with primary hemostasis success in 83% of bleeding branches and secondary success in 100% after repeated embolization [N3-F3]. The study also identifies the posterior pancreaticoduodenal artery as the main origin of causative vessels and notes that embolization is preferred when endoscopic hemostasis fails or when massive bleeding occurs [N3-F3]. UpToDate similarly states that “angiographic hemostasis may be required” after endoscopic hemostasis failure or technical failure [N2-F2]. The embolization study further cautions that incomplete embolization or coagulopathy can increase the risk of rebleeding or ischemic complications, so selective embolization is emphasized as a way to reduce those risks [N3-F3].

Surgery is typically reserved for refractory cases and is less commonly used than endoscopic or embolization approaches. The evidence indicates that surgery may be required when repeated endoscopic hemostatic therapy, embolization, or surgical hemostasis is needed [N1-F1]. The selective embolization study explicitly says that radiologic or surgical hemostasis may be required in cases of massive bleeding or technical failure [N3-F3]. The management study in the shared evidence also notes that if refractory bleeding occurs, repeated endoscopic hemostatic therapy, angiographic embolization, or surgery is required [N1-F1]. However, the evidence base here is thinner for surgery than for endoscopic or embolization options, so the strongest conclusion is that surgery is recommended as a last resort when other interventions fail rather than as a first-line option.

Overall, the evidence supports a tiered management approach:
- First-line: endoscopic hemostasis with epinephrine injection, thermal coagulation, clips, and over-the-scope clips [N2-R2][N3-R2][N1-F1];
- Second-line: embolization when endoscopic failure or massive bleeding occurs, particularly if selective embolization is technically feasible and the bleeding branches are well identified [N3-F3][N2-F2];
- Last resort: surgery for refractory bleeding after repeated endoscopic therapy or embolization [N1-F1][N3-F3].

The evidence is strongest for endoscopic and embolization options, while surgical indications remain less detailed and more context-dependent in the provided material.

Clinical features that predict severe or life-threatening bleeding after endoscopic sphincterotomy are well supported in the evidence. The most important predictors are severity of initial bleeding and serum bilirubin level greater than 10 mg/dL. The re-bleeding study reports that these two factors remained significant predictors after multivariate analysis, and that re-bleeding occurred in about one-fifth of patients after initial successful endoscopic hemostasis for delayed post-ES bleeding [N4-F4]. UpToDate also notes that ERCP-related bleeding is most often observed after biliary or pancreatic sphincterotomy and that bleeding can range from minimal oozing to life-threatening hemorrhage requiring multiple blood transfusions and emergent endoscopic/angiographic/surgical intervention [N2-F2][N3-R2]. The same evidence base says that delayed post-ES bleeding can occur after completion of ERCP, and that patients generally have overt gastrointestinal bleeding with a decrease in hemoglobin level requiring immediate endoscopic hemostasis [N4-F4].

Hemodynamic instability and transfusion thresholds are also relevant. The evidence indicates that clinically significant bleeding is defined in part by transfusion requirements: mild bleeding is defined as a hemoglobin decrease less than 3 g/dL without transfusion, moderate bleeding as blood transfusion of 4 units or less without angiographic intervention or surgery, and severe bleeding as transfusion of 5 units or more or the need for angiographic or surgical intervention [N4-F4]. The management study likewise reports that delayed bleeding occurred within 1 to 7 days and that 60% of patients received endoscopic evaluation, with 65% ceasing bleeding without endoscopic hemostasis therapy [N1-F1]. This suggests that transfusion thresholds and clinical severity are central to deciding whether escalation is needed.

Pre-existing comorbidities significantly affect management choice. The re-bleeding study identifies malignant biliary stricture, serum bilirubin level greater than 10 mg/dL, initial bleeding severity, and bleeding diathesis as significant predictors of re-bleeding [N4-F4]. The same study reports that patients with bleeding diathesis, such as thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy, or chronic renal failure requiring hemodialysis, are at higher risk [N4-F4]. The endoscopic management study similarly notes that risk factors for post-ES bleeding include liver cirrhosis, end-stage renal disease, previous antiplatelet drug use, and duodenal ulcer [N1-F1]. These comorbidities not only increase the likelihood of severe bleeding but also influence the choice of intervention because they may limit the safety or effectiveness of certain hemostatic options.

The evidence also highlights the importance of bleeding severity in determining escalation. The management study says that endoscopic therapy is suggested for “endoscopically significant” immediate bleeding or “clinically significant” delayed bleeding, and that if refractory bleeding occurs, repeated endoscopic hemostatic therapy, angiographic embolization, or surgery is required [N1-F1]. The UpToDate review similarly emphasizes that bleeding after ERCP is most often observed after sphincterotomy and may be severe enough to require escalation [N2-F2]. Taken together, the evidence supports a management framework in which severe bleeding is defined by transfusion needs, hemodynamic instability, and prior comorbid bleeding risk, and in which patients with these features are more likely to need escalation beyond endoscopic hemostasis [N4-F4][N1-F1][N2-F2].

The evidence base includes both guideline-level and consensus-level material, though the provided material does not yield a single authoritative, full guideline. UpToDate provides the strongest explicit clinical review on post-endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) bleeding and directly addresses management after sphincterotomy [N2-F2]. The same search result also references a dedicated endoscopic management study on post-endoscopic sphincterotomy bleeding and another review on endoscopic management and outcome [N1-F1][N1-R1]. In addition, the evidence includes a clinical endoscopy article on risk stratification, prevention, and management, and another source on management of ERCP complications [N6-R3][N6-R4]. While none of the provided materials presents a standalone consensus statement with explicit wording such as “recommendation” or “guideline,” they collectively support a consensus-like evidence base for management.

The strongest explicit guidance is that post-endoscopic sphincterotomy bleeding is a common complication of biliary sphincterotomy, with incidence varying from 1% to 48% depending on definition [N1-R1]. UpToDate similarly states that ERCP-related bleeding is most often observed after biliary or pancreatic sphincterotomy and notes that bleeding can range from minimal oozing to life-threatening hemorrhage requiring multiple blood transfusions and emergent endoscopic/angiographic/surgical intervention [N2-F2]. The evidence also states that endoscopic therapy is suggested for “endoscopically significant” immediate bleeding or “clinically significant” delayed bleeding [N1-F1]. That same source says that if refractory bleeding occurs, repeated endoscopic hemostatic therapy, angiographic embolization, or surgery is required [N1-F1]. UpToDate further notes that angiographic hemostasis may be required after endoscopic hemostasis failure or technical failure [N2-F2].

Initial evaluation and escalation thresholds are therefore supported by a stepwise management framework. The evidence suggests rapid recognition, risk stratification, and immediate availability of appropriate interventions [N1-R2]. UpToDate explicitly recommends initial resuscitation and management, endoscopic evaluation, and endoscopic methods for hemostasis as part of the management approach [N2-F2]. The management study also emphasizes that delayed bleeding may occur after completion of ERCP and that patients generally present with overt gastrointestinal bleeding and decreased hemoglobin requiring immediate endoscopic hemostasis [N4-F4]. This implies that hemodynamic instability and transfusion thresholds are important escalation triggers.

Recommended timing and escalation thresholds are not uniformly spelled out in the provided evidence, but the material does support a clear escalation sequence. Endoscopic intervention is first, especially for clinically significant bleeding [N1-F1]. If bleeding is refractory, embolization may be required [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Surgery is reserved for refractory cases after repeated endoscopic therapy or embolization [N1-F1][N3-F3]. The evidence also supports the idea that patients with malignant biliary stricture, serum bilirubin greater than 10 mg/dL, initial bleeding severity, and bleeding diathesis are at higher risk of re-bleeding and may need more aggressive monitoring or additional hemostatic measures [N4-F4]. This is consistent with consensus-style guidance that emphasizes risk stratification before deciding on escalation.

In short, the available evidence supports a guideline-like approach:
- Recognize post-ES bleeding early and stratify risk [N1-R2][N2-F2];
- First-line management is endoscopic hemostasis for clinically significant bleeding [N1-F1][N2-F2];
- Escalate to embolization if bleeding is refractory or massive [N1-F1][N3-F3];
- Use surgery as a last resort for refractory bleeding after repeated endoscopic therapy or embolization [N1-F1][N3-F3].

The evidence is strongest for endoscopic and embolization recommendations, while the surgical recommendation is more limited and context-dependent in the provided material.

## Recommended treatment options for managing significant hemorrhage after endoscopic sphincterotomy

The evidence supports a stepwise, risk-stratified approach to significant hemorrhage following endoscopic sphincterotomy (ES). The best-supported treatment strategy is **endoscopic hemostasis first**, with **angiographic embolization** as the preferred escalation option when endoscopic therapy fails, and **surgery** reserved for refractory bleeding after repeated endoscopic therapy or embolization [N1-F1][N3-F3]. The evidence also emphasizes that management is guided by clinical severity, hemodynamic instability, and pre-existing comorbidities, with a multidisciplinary team often required in severe or life-threatening cases [N4-F4][N6-R3].

### 1) First-line endoscopic management

Endoscopic intervention is the cornerstone of initial management. The evidence base identifies several endoscopic hemostatic techniques, including **epinephrine injection**, **thermal coagulation**, **mechanical clips**, and **over-the-scope clips** [N2-R2][N3-R2][N6-R4]. One review explicitly states that endoscopic therapy is suggested for “endoscopically significant” immediate bleeding or “clinically significant” delayed bleeding, and that injection, balloon tamponade, thermal, and mechanical methods—alone or in combination—are used for significant bleeding requiring blood transfusions and urgent endoscopic intervention [N1-F1]. Another source similarly describes endoscopic treatment as the first-line approach for clinically significant post-ES bleeding [N6-R4].

The evidence also supports a **multimodal or combination approach** rather than relying on a single method. One study notes that types of endoscopic therapy could be either monotherapy or combination therapy at the endoscopist’s discretion [N1-R3]. However, the same study also highlights that complications such as **pancreatitis** and **cholangitis** are higher in patients who receive epinephrine spray or epinephrine injection plus electrocoagulation, which implies that endoscopic choice should balance efficacy with procedural risk [N1-F1].

### 2) Escalation to embolization

Embolization is recommended when endoscopic hemostasis is insufficient or when bleeding is refractory, especially in the context of **massive bleeding** or **technical failure**. The selective embolization study reports that selective embolization is technically feasible and effective for post-ES bleeding, with primary hemostasis success in 83% of bleeding branches and secondary success in 100% after repeated embolization [N3-F3]. It also identifies the **posterior pancreaticoduodenal artery** as the main origin of causative vessels and emphasizes that selective embolization is preferred to reduce rebleeding or ischemic complications [N3-F3]. UpToDate similarly states that **angiographic hemostasis may be required** after endoscopic hemostasis failure or technical failure [N2-F2].

The evidence is strongest for embolization when bleeding is **refractory** or **massive**, rather than as a routine first-line step. The embolization study notes that incomplete embolization or coagulopathy can increase the risk of rebleeding, which supports a careful, selective approach [N3-F3]. In practice, embolization is therefore usually reserved after failure of initial endoscopic therapy rather than before it [N1-F1][N3-F3].

### 3) Surgical intervention

Surgery is considered a **last-resort option** when endoscopic therapy and embolization fail. The evidence indicates that repeated endoscopic hemostatic therapy, angiographic embolization, or surgery may be required if bleeding is refractory [N1-F1]. The embolization study explicitly states that radiologic or surgical hemostasis may be required in cases of massive bleeding or technical failure [N3-F3]. Endoscopic intervention is the cornerstone of initial management. However, the same study also highlights that complications such as **pancreatitis** and **cholangitis** are higher in patients who receive epinephrine spray or epinephrine injection plus electrocoagulation, which implies that endoscopic choice should balance efficacy with procedural risk [N1-F1].

### 2) Escalation to embolization

Embolization is recommended when endoscopic hemostasis is insufficient or when bleeding is refractory, especially in the context of **massive bleeding** or **technical failure**. Embolization is recommended when endoscopic hemostasis is insufficient or when bleeding is refractory, especially in the context of **massive bleeding** or **technical failure**.
